name: Grammar From the Class's Own Errors
title: Grammar From the Class's Own Errors
answer: Grammar instruction works best when it targets the errors a class actually makes, rather than following a fixed sequence. A teacher can collect anonymous sentences from student drafts, have an AI tool sort the errors by type, and then teach short lessons on the two or three most common ones. This matters because it spends limited lesson time on what students genuinely need and turns grammar tools into occasions for learning rules.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea is about building grammar lessons from the real mistakes found in a class's own writing. Instead of teaching grammar in the abstract, the teacher gathers sentences from student drafts, strips out anything that identifies the writer, and uses an AI tool to group the errors by category. The grouped results reveal which problems are widespread across the class, such as comma splices or disagreements between subject and verb. The teacher then designs brief lessons around the two or three error types that matter most. The problem it solves is wasted time on grammar points that few students struggle with, while the errors that actually weaken their writing go unaddressed.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a teacher collects a set of sentences from drafts, removes names and other identifying details, and asks an AI tool to sort the errors into types. The tool's output shows which errors recur across the class, and the teacher picks the two or three most common for short lessons. The text does not give separate grade band examples, so the same routine applies from kindergarten through twelfth grade, with the sentences and error types suited to the class. After a brief lesson on a common error, students practice it in their own writing. Students can also be asked to accept or reject each suggestion from a grammar tool and explain their choice for a few sentences, which turns a correction tool into a learning tool.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the research here as urging caution. A study of 119 high school students found that feedback on writing strategies combined with revision improved essays, while spelling and grammar checkers added only small gains on some measures (McCarthy et al., 2022). The text draws the conclusion that grammar matters but is not where most improvement in writing comes from. It adds that a brief lesson on a common error, followed by practice in the student's own writing, is usually enough.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits. Grammar is not the main source of improvement in writing, so lessons built from class errors should stay brief and should not crowd out work on writing strategies and revision. Students who accept every suggestion from a grammar tool learn little, so teachers should ask them to accept or reject each suggestion and explain their reasoning for a few sentences. The decisions about which errors to teach, how to anonymize student sentences, and how to frame the tool's suggestions remain with the teacher. Nothing here is legal advice, and the practice described is instructional rather than a compliance measure.
